query: Which method can be used for phase stability, microstructure refinement, and property optimization, and why?

generation.hypothesis: High‐throughput computational screening integrated with tailored thermal treatments (homogenization and annealing) can be used to achieve phase stability, microstructure refinement, and optimized mechanical properties in high‐entropy alloys by promoting the formation of finely dispersed nanoscale precipitates.
generation.material_initial_state: Multicomponent high‐entropy alloy systems (e.g., the Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti system prepared by arc melting) with a mixed BCC matrix and potential for L21 phase formation.
generation.intervention: Use high‐throughput computational screening to identify compositions with favorable phase stability (e.g., targeted L21 phase fraction and high melting temperature) and then apply controlled thermal treatments (e.g., homogenization at high temperature followed by annealing at lower temperature) to achieve the desired nanoscale precipitate microstructure.
generation.conditions: Processing conditions similar to arc melting, homogenization at ~1200 °C, and annealing at ~700 °C for 2 hours under conditions that promote compositional homogeneity and controlled precipitate formation; applicable within composition ranges where Al <25 at.% and Mn >15 at.%.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale L21 precipitates or ordered antiphase domains embedded within a softer BCC matrix that enable load transfer and ordering strengthening.
generation.mechanism: The computational screening guides selection of compositions that thermodynamically favor the formation of ordered precipitates, while the controlled thermal treatments restrict excessive coarsening. This leads to a refined microstructure in which the fine precipitates impede dislocation motion and transfer load, thereby boosting mechanical properties, especially at elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to conventionally processed alloys, the screening‐guided and thermally treated alloys will exhibit a finer, more uniform distribution of nanoscale precipitates, leading to significantly improved high‐temperature yield strength (e.g., an increase on the order of 100 MPa or more under similar test conditions).
generation.baseline: High‐entropy alloys produced without computational screening and controlled thermal treatments typically display less refined precipitate structures and lower mechanical performance at high temperatures.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold within the identified compositional window and for processing routes that allow precise control of homogenization and annealing; outside these regimes or with significant compositional deviations, the benefits may not be realized.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the yield strength improvement and precise precipitate size distributions are sensitive to minor variations in composition and processing conditions; moreover, uncertainties in the thermodynamic database may affect optimal processing windows.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloys using the same base HEA system: one set with compositions chosen by high‐throughput computational screening followed by precise homogenization and annealing, and a control set prepared using conventional composition selection and processing. Characterize both sets using TEM and XRD for precipitate morphology and phase stability, and perform high‐temperature compression tests (e.g., at 600–700 °C).
measurements: Nanoscale precipitate size and number density (via TEM)
Phase identification and lattice parameters (via XRD)
Yield strength and other mechanical properties at elevated temperatures (via compression tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the screening‐guided, thermally treated alloys do not demonstrate a statistically significant refinement of the microstructure (i.e., finer, uniformly distributed precipitates) and corresponding improvement in high‐temperature mechanical properties (e.g., yield strength difference less than the experimental uncertainty) compared to the control, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Paper card. Question: How can high-throughput computational screening be used to discover lightweight, precipitation-strengthened high-entropy alloys with high-temperature strength superior to traditional ferritic superalloys?. System: Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti quinary system (specifically Al20Cr5Fe50Mn20Ti5 and Al15Cr5Fe50Mn25Ti5 as successful cases). Processing: Arc-melting of 99.9 wt% purity constituent elements, melted at least six times for homogeneity, followed by drop-casting; subsequent homogenization at 1200 °C and annealing at 700 °C for 2 hours for specific characterizations. Test conditions: Compression tests at room temperature and elevated temperatures (up to 700 °C) at a strain rate of 2 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹; in situ neutron scattering from room temperature to 1050 °C; synchrotron XRD and TEM characterization.
